title: Ramesh Damani & Mohnish Pabrai Q&A with Millennium Mams' - May 8, 2020
summary: A pandemic-era conversation with Ramesh Damani for a group of Indian women investors. Pabrai stresses the basics of compounding (spend less than you earn, index and dollar-cost average over decades), explains why he is cautious and building cash given the disconnect between markets and a real economy with 33 million US unemployment claims, and discusses Nick Sleep, Li Lu, Buffett and Munger's bearishness, US-China tensions, India's missed manufacturing opportunity, gold, Bitcoin, and Richard Koo's book on why money printing did not cause inflation.

ideas.idea: Financially literate women are the cornerstone of household wealth because 'spend less than you earn' is largely in their hands, which is why Dakshana is more excited to support a girl than a boy.
ideas.detail: Supporting a girl impacts the whole family and several generations, the same reason Grameen Bank went with women; savings driven by women become the foundation for compounding.

ideas.idea: Compounding has three variables, capital, length of runway and rate of return, and a long runway makes a high return unnecessary.
ideas.detail: 50% a year for five years and 5% a year for 50 years give almost interchangeable results, so starting very early matters more than heroic returns or even the amount of capital.

ideas.idea: Ordinary families do not need to understand companies; consistent long-term index investing and dollar-cost averaging over decades will deliver great returns.
ideas.detail: He strongly encourages the Millennium Mams to index, since most of their wealth sits in their families' future earning power; wealthy Indian families should also use the $250,000 annual remittance allowance to get S&P 500 exposure to the Amazons and Microsofts of the world.

ideas.idea: Heroes should not be limited to the living; most of his learning from Buffett and Munger came from reading, not from knowing them, and one's parents are the greatest heroes.
ideas.detail: Munger says the eminent dead are some of the best heroes; Pabrai got a tremendous head start from both parents and picks up different things from many people.

ideas.idea: Nick Sleep returned all investor capital rather than keep charging fees on a three-stock portfolio of Amazon, Berkshire and Costco, and that portfolio turned out to be Corona-proof.
ideas.detail: Sleep ran north of a billion dollars, held the three stocks for over 10 years, told investors to buy them directly, and gave up hundreds of millions in future fees; only Buffett has otherwise shut down a partnership, and he did it because prices were too high.

ideas.idea: The biggest lesson from the 2020 Berkshire meeting was that Buffett did not go shopping and even said Berkshire's cash cushion is not that high given the range of outcomes.
ideas.detail: Munger described them as a ship captain in the worst tempest whose objective is to get to the other side safely; Berkshire was a net seller of equities over four months and exited the airlines, which Pabrai calls a no-brainer.

ideas.idea: There is a huge disconnect between the real economy and equity markets, so building cash is not a bad idea even if the gloom scenarios never play out.
ideas.detail: More than 33 million Americans, over 20% of the workforce, filed for unemployment, possibly surpassing the Great Depression's 25% peak, yet markets brushed it off; Buffett noted the real 1929 decline of 85% came over the following two years after an initial rebound. On a desert island hearing only the economic news he would have guessed the Sensex and Dow were down 50-70%.

ideas.idea: Most businesses are extremely fragile creations that cannot pay staff for even 30-45 days without revenue, so the small-business damage from the pandemic is huge and warrants caution.
ideas.detail: Businesses earn a few percentage points of profit under brutal competition; Bill Gates wanted Microsoft to hold enough cash to pay staff for two years with no revenue, which almost no business can do.

ideas.idea: Li Lu is a Swiss-army-knife investor with unusual wiring who, like Buffett and Munger, focuses first on what can go wrong, then on long runways and entrepreneurs, and holds for 15-20 years.
ideas.detail: Munger introduced them 11 years ago and insisted they lunch monthly. Li Lu, a Tiananmen leader smuggled out of China, did three Columbia degrees in four years and made his first million investing the float on his student loans.

ideas.idea: When Buffett, Munger and Li Lu are all bearish, the right response is to pay attention even if you do not fully understand their reasons.
ideas.detail: Their intellect is beyond human intellect; second- and third-order effects of the pandemic (hospitals laying off staff as elective procedures stop, CVS prescriptions down, finely tuned auto supply chains breaking) are hard to forecast.

ideas.idea: The pandemic differs from other crises in having a definitive end date, perhaps 15-18 months away, but the have-nots lose first and wealth polarization will worsen.
ideas.detail: The have-nots have the least staying power and savings and were the first to lose jobs, globally and in India.

ideas.idea: A rising power has never challenged an incumbent peacefully, and US-China relations are at a multi-decade low, so the range of outcomes is wide with ugly outliers.
ideas.detail: The US has valid grievances since trade with China was unfair, but it benevolently allowed it (Marshall Plan, favorable deals) to help the world rise; countries will now rebuild medical supply chains and stockpiles so US dependence on China and India for medicines falls within 10 years. Long run, the world needs China and China needs the world.

ideas.idea: India dropped the ball big time on capturing manufacturing leaving China; Vietnam is running out of labor while almost no work moved to India.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Red tape and bureaucracy make India hard for multinationals despite a favored US relationship and Trump-Modi rapport; passive investments by Facebook, Silver Lake and the Saudis in Reliance Jio are exceptions, not the holy grail of a bicycle maker relocating production to India. Rule changes after Walmart's Flipkart deal illustrate the problem.

ideas.idea: India grows while the government sleeps; the private sector delivers (Jio, aviation, mobile) but the government fails on physical infrastructure like rail and power.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: India's rail track has barely grown since 1947 while China laid tens of thousands of kilometers of high-speed track; Dakshana Valley in Pune lacks three-phase power four days a week while power plants sit idle. A benevolent dictatorship would be better but the odds are against a dictator being benevolent.

ideas.idea: The Chinese people gave the Communist Party a long rope and it has delivered growth impossible in a democracy, but tension will rise as prosperity makes citizens want more than economics.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Most Chinese would agree the growth would not have happened under democracy; society has so far accepted the price in freedom of speech.

ideas.idea: His entry into India has been unwise so far, with far better outcomes in China and the US, but he expects his Indian investments to do very well over five to ten years.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: India's positives are a great class of entrepreneurs, improving governance, pent-up demand and a demographic dividend (average age 28), which he also expects to blunt COVID mortality; the big 'if' is government-provided infrastructure and education.

ideas.idea: It is dangerous for individuals to act on stock names; a great business is not necessarily a great investment because the entry price determines investor returns.
ideas.detail: Amazon will do well but buying at a trillion-dollar cap is a different question; Jio is an incredible dominant business but returns from today differ from 10 or 20 years ago. He declined to disclose his portfolio for this reason.

ideas.idea: In 2000 he warned Microsoft's Indian executives that holding the stock at a $600 billion cap earning under $10 billion would end badly, and it went nowhere for 15 years despite the business growing.
ideas.detail: They had 95% of net worth in Microsoft and had never seen it decline; the stock fell 50-60% and was flat until 2013-14, and the money they put in Pabrai Funds did far better.

ideas.idea: Gold is a non-productive asset, an 80-foot cube that stays the same size for 100 years; buy jewelry to enjoy but do not invest family assets in it.
ideas.detail: He recounts Buffett's Martian analogy; gold and real estate have not been the straight rides Indians assumed, and Indian women are moving toward equity markets, a shift he expects to continue.

ideas.idea: Bitcoin has no long-term value; he sold the one Bitcoin a VC friend gifted him at $4-5,000 when it reached $19,000 and the rest at $12-13,000.
ideas.detail: Two hours with a Forbes-profiled Bitcoin billionaire did not change his view; he told the friend to unload his billion and put an end to the ride, and files Bitcoin in the too-hard pile.

ideas.idea: Richard Koo's 'The Other Half of Macroeconomics', recommended by Li Lu, is the only credible explanation for why Fed money printing did not cause inflation, and it may not this time either.
ideas.detail: He thinks the Fed printing money now is the right thing to do and it is unclear inflation will follow; most books could be 10 pages and the first 30-40 pages of Koo's suffice.

ideas.idea: US stimulus must be seen against household wealth: America is a $100 trillion family that can spend $5-10 trillion without feeling it.
ideas.detail: Global household wealth is about $400 trillion, $100 trillion of it in the US versus $22 trillion GDP; US household wealth was 50-55 trillion in 2009. Jerome Powell may go down as one of the greatest Fed governors for unprecedented actions like buying commercial paper directly.

ideas.idea: Poor Charlie's Almanack, especially the Psychology of Human Misjudgment on pages 440-494, is the number one book because understanding human quirkiness gives a leg up in life and relationships.
ideas.detail: He rereads that talk every year; Munger took 50-60 years to distil that wisdom and is endlessly curious about how humans work, even Pabrai's dysfunctional relatives at their last dinner on March 7, 2020.

ideas.idea: At the charity lunch Buffett told his daughters the single most important decision in life is whom you marry.
ideas.detail: The lunch ran over three hours with more than 50 questions; his daughters, then 10 and 12, still remember the advice, and it makes a massive difference for women who often get the shortest straw.

ideas.idea: Buffett is 'just a kid': he barely uses a cell phone, eats what he ate at five, and plays the game like Monopoly, which is the most accurate description of him.
ideas.detail: Lunches with his assistant Debbie were more revealing than lunch with Buffett; he keeps his phone in her drawer, and on an impromptu tour of Berkshire headquarters he showed memorabilia and a foot-high strawberry milkshake lunch.
